locate.title: Locate the Detained Person
locate.description: Use the official ICE detainee locator to find out where the person is being held.
locate.guidance:
The ICE Detainee Locator (locator.ice.gov) is the official government tool for locating detained individuals. Searches can be done by name and date of birth, or by A-Number.

How to search:
1. Go to locator.ice.gov
2. Choose to search by name or by A-Number (if known)
3. For a name search, enter first and last name in English letters, country of birth, and date of birth
4. For an A-Number search, enter the nine-digit number without the letter A
5. Click Search and wait for results

Common result statuses:
- "Call ICE For Details" — this typically means the person was recently transferred or is in initial processing. Call the ICE detainee hotline: 1-888-351-4024. Have the full name, date of birth, and A-Number (if known) ready.
- "Not Found" — try alternate spellings (especially names transliterated from other scripts). If the arrest was recent (less than 72 hours ago), the person may not yet appear in the database. Transfers between facilities in the first 72 hours are common. Call the hotline.
- Facility found — write down the exact name, address, and phone number. This information is needed for letters, calls, and mail.

If searches return no result after multiple attempts, contact a local nonprofit immigration organization — they often have additional search resources.
tips: Try both accented and unaccented versions of names (e.g., José and Jose)
Transfers in the first 72 hours are routine. If the person is not found today, try again tomorrow
Take a screenshot of the search result with date and time — useful for tracking transfers
The ICE detainee hotline is available 24 hours: 1-888-351-4024

three_rules.title: Three Rules for the Detained Person
three_rules.description: General information about what detained individuals commonly do and avoid — not advice about any specific action.
three_rules.guidance:
Families often ask what to communicate to a detained family member. The following is publicly available general information published by immigrant rights organizations.

Rule 1: Do not sign documents without understanding them
Families commonly report that detained individuals sometimes experience pressure to sign "Voluntary Departure" documents. Immigration attorneys emphasize that anyone held in detention should consult with an attorney before signing any legal documents. Voluntary Departure has legal consequences that are important to understand beforehand.

Rule 2: Accurately state the period of US residence
If asked during any interview about the length of time spent in the US, it is generally important to state the actual years of physical presence accurately. Attorneys note that documented residency history is often a key factor in the evaluation of a case.

Rule 3: Share concerns about returning to the home country
If a person has fears or concerns about returning to their country of origin, this is information that is important for an attorney to know. Immigrant rights organizations advise communicating these concerns to an attorney as early as possible — before any hearings.

Note: This is general information, not legal advice. Every person's situation is unique, and only a licensed attorney can evaluate the legal dimensions of a specific situation.
tips: Pass this information to the detained person at the first opportunity — by letter or during a phone call
ILRC and ACLU publish free materials on detained persons' rights in multiple languages
Keep a written log of every contact with the detained person, including date and topics discussed
If an attorney is involved, help facilitate contact with the detained person as quickly as possible

money_calls.title: Money & Phone Calls
money_calls.description: How to set up a calling account and send money to the detained person.
money_calls.guidance:
Most ICE facilities use commercial operators for telephone calls and inmate accounts. The most common systems are Telmate and GTL (Global Tel Link).

For Adelanto and many other California facilities, the system used is Telmate.

How to set up calls through Telmate:
1. Go to telmate.com or download the Telmate app on your smartphone
2. Click "Create Account" and register as "Friends & Family"
3. Verify your email address
4. Add the detained person: enter their name and facility (or PIN if already known)
5. Fund your account with a debit or credit card, or through PayNearMe (can be paid in cash at CVS, 7-Eleven, and other stores)
6. Call costs: typically $0.06 to $0.14 per minute for domestic calls. Rates may vary.

Sending money to the detainee's commissary account (for purchases at the facility store):
- Through the same operator's website (Telmate, GTL)
- Through JPay (used at some facilities)
- Through Western Union in some cases
- Confirm the specific system with the facility by phone

Practical notes:
- Write down the detained person's PIN after first contact — it is needed for adding funds
- Calls may be recorded. Do not discuss legal strategy on the phone — only through an attorney
- If the person is transferred to a different facility, funds in the account may not transfer automatically. Check the operator's policy.
tips: Save receipts for all transactions — helpful if there are technical problems
The Telmate app for iOS and Android lets you see balances in real time
Calls from the facility are typically outgoing from the detained person to you, not the other way around
For PayNearMe, you will receive a link by text message — take it to a participating store to pay in cash

mail_format.title: Mailing Format
mail_format.description: How to correctly address mail so that it reaches the detained person.
mail_format.guidance:
Correct address format is critical — mail without an A-Number frequently does not reach the recipient.

Standard format for most ICE facilities:
[Detained person's full name]
[A-Number]
[Facility name]
[Facility address]

Example for Adelanto:
Ivan Petrov
A123 456 789
Adelanto ICE Processing Center
10250 Rancho Road
Adelanto, CA 92301

What typically gets through:
- Regular letters and postcards
- Photographs (generally no more than 5 per envelope, no staples)
- Printed materials (books, magazines) — generally only directly from a publisher or bookstore
- Religious materials (Bible, Quran, etc.) — generally permitted; confirm with the facility

What typically does not get through:
- Gum, candy, food items
- Stickers, staples, paper clips, binder clips
- Colored envelopes or envelopes with metallic elements
- Envelopes with perfume or other substances

Legal Mail:
- Letters from an attorney carry a special status and must only be opened in the detainee's presence
- The attorney should mark the envelope "LEGAL MAIL — ATTORNEY-CLIENT PRIVILEGED"
- If the facility violates this, the attorney can file a complaint

It is advisable to call or write the facility directly to confirm current mail rules — they can change.
tips: Always write the A-Number on the envelope — it is the most important identifier
Allow 7–10 business days before considering a letter lost
If the facility uses electronic messaging (Telmate Messages), this may be faster
Keep copies of all important letters you send

attorney.title: Finding an Attorney
attorney.description: How to vet an attorney and avoid fraud.
attorney.guidance:
Finding a trustworthy immigration attorney is one of the most important steps. The following is general information about how families commonly check attorneys' credentials.

How to check an attorney in California:
1. Confirm the person is a licensed attorney (not a notary or "immigration consultant")
2. Check the license at the California State Bar website: calbar.ca.gov — enter the name and verify status
3. Check the EOIR (Immigration Court) list of disciplinary actions: justice.gov/eoir/discipline-of-practitioners
4. Look for reviews on Google, Avvo, or in local immigrant community networks

Red flags for fraud:
- Demand for a large cash payment upfront without a written agreement
- Guarantees of results ("100% win", "guaranteed no deportation")
- Calls themselves a "notario" — in the US, a notary public does not have legal authority to practice law
- Refuses to provide a written contract or answer questions about strategy
- Does not explain strategy or communicate case updates

Questions to ask at a consultation:
- How many immigration cases did you handle last year?
- Have you had cases similar to this one?
- What are the general options available — not guarantees, just options?
- How often will you update us on the case status?
- What are your fees and how do you bill?

Free or low-cost legal help:
Many nonprofit organizations provide free or low-cost legal help for detained individuals. Search: immigration-locator.thekennedyforum.org or contact a local Legal Aid office.

Note: An attorney has a professional responsibility to their client. If there are concerns about conduct, a complaint can be filed with the State Bar.
tips: A list of pro bono immigration attorneys in California is available at ilrc.org or ailalawyer.com
Do not pay without signing a written retainer agreement that specifies fees and scope of services
Many consultations cost $100 to $300 — this is normal and worthwhile for screening an attorney
If an attorney promises a guaranteed outcome, treat it as a warning sign

sources.label: California State Bar — Check a license

evidence_kickoff.title: Starting Document Collection
evidence_kickoff.description: What documents attorneys commonly request and how to organize them by category.
evidence_kickoff.guidance:
Document collection is a lengthy process — starting early is one of the most helpful things a family can do. The following is general information about what documents attorneys commonly request when evaluating immigration cases.

Note: The specific document list depends on the facts of the case and is determined by an attorney. This information is general in nature.

Common document categories:

1. Tax Returns
- W-2 forms, 1040 returns for every year since entry into the US
- If returns were not filed, attorneys can explain how to obtain IRS records

2. Housing Documents
- Lease agreements, rent receipts, property deeds
- Utility bills with name and address for each year
- Bank statements, government mail showing address history

3. School Records
- Enrollment records, report cards, diplomas for children in the US
- Personal academic records if applicable

4. Medical Records
- Doctor's notes, bills, insurance cards
- Medical documents for US citizen children are often particularly relevant

5. Bank Statements
- Account statements for each year of presence in the US

6. Employment Records
- Employment contracts, employer letters, pay stubs
- Business registration documents if self-employed

7. ID and Vital Records
- Passport, driver's license, foreign identity documents
- Children's birth certificates
- Marriage or divorce certificates

8. Photos with Dates
- Photos with family, at events, in different US locations with dates
- Printed digital photos with metadata or handwritten captions

9. Other Documents
- Church or community organization membership records
- Volunteer letters
- Other evidence of continuous presence in the US

Organizing documents:
- Create a folder for each year (e.g., "2015", "2016", etc.)
- Make color copies or photographs of originals
- Keep digital copies in a secure cloud location
- Use this application's Evidence Builder module to organize records
tips: Start with tax returns — they are among the easiest to retrieve through IRS.gov (Get Transcript tool)
Ask friends and family to look for shared photographs with dates
Utility companies can often provide multi-year billing history — call customer service
Do not discard documents that seem minor — an attorney will determine what is relevant

sources.label: IRS Get My Tax Record (transcript copies)

support_letters.title: Support Letters
support_letters.description: Who can write a support letter and what such letters commonly include.
support_letters.guidance:
Support letters from community members, employers, and others are often an important part of the documentation that attorneys present in immigration proceedings. The following is general information about what these letters commonly contain.

Who can write a letter:
- Employers and coworkers
- Neighbors and friends
- Pastors, priests, imams, and other religious leaders
- Teachers and school principals (especially from schools the children attend)
- Community organization leaders
- Sports team coaches
- Physicians (if the detained person is the primary caregiver of an ill family member)

What these letters commonly include:
- How long the author has known the detained person (specific years)
- In what capacity — neighbor, employer, fellow church member, etc.
- Specific examples of character, community contribution, reliability
- How the detention has affected the family and community
- The author's contact information for verification

Format:
- On official letterhead is preferable (for employers and organizations)
- Signed and dated
- In English, or with a notarized translation
- No specific legal format is required — a sincere, personal letter is sufficient

An attorney typically advises how many letters are needed and from whom. Coordinate this process with the attorney if one is already involved.
tips: Ask people from different areas of life — work, church, neighbors, school
Specific details matter more than general praise: 'Ivan worked for me for 5 years' is more useful than 'he is a good person'
Organize the collection of letters early — this process typically takes several weeks
Letters in other languages also need to be translated into English

children_care.title: Documents for Children
children_care.description: What documents related to US citizen or LPR children attorneys commonly find relevant.
children_care.guidance:
US citizen children or children with lawful permanent resident status are often relevant factors in immigration cases. The following is general information about what documents families commonly gather in these situations. Only an attorney can evaluate how these documents may be significant in a specific case.

Children's birth certificates:
- US birth certificates for all minor children
- If children were born abroad and have citizenship or LPR status — the relevant documents

School records:
- Enrollment and attendance records
- Report cards, certificates, and awards
- Letters from teachers or the school principal
- IEP or special needs documentation (if applicable)

Medical records for children:
- Medical records and history
- Documentation of chronic conditions or special medical needs
- Doctor's note regarding the detained person's role in the child's care

Financial documents:
- Evidence that the detained person is the primary financial provider
- Receipts for school meals, extracurricular activities, medical services

Custody in case of extended absence:
- If there is risk of a prolonged absence, families sometimes arrange a notarized power of attorney for custody
- An attorney or local Legal Aid office can assist with this
- Discuss temporary custody arrangements with an attorney while the case is pending

Psychological impact on children:
- Some attorneys request letters from a psychologist or school counselor about the impact of detention on a child
- This is not a standard requirement but may be relevant in some situations
tips: Gather documents for all children in the family, regardless of their immigration status
Medical records showing that the detained person is the child's primary caregiver are often important
If children are in school, ask their teacher to write a letter about the parent's role in the child's life
A notarized power of attorney for custody protects children while the case is pending

sources.label: ILRC — Children's rights in immigration cases
